The Token-Efficiency Frontier: A practical framework for PMs shipping with LLMs

Every product team using LLMs eventually hits the same wall. They want better answers, longer context, smarter agents, and they want it for less. The instinct is to negotiate on one knob at a time: switch to a cheaper model, trim the prompt, batch the calls. That instinct is wrong. The trade-off is not a line. It is a frontier, and once you see it, the entire way you budget tokens, plan features, and write PRs changes.

The hidden cost beneath the chat window

Most PMs treat tokens the way they treat cloud storage: a bill that arrives monthly, mostly out of sight, mostly fine until it isn't. That framing is broken. Tokens are not storage. They are a live substrate for every product decision involving generation, retrieval, and reasoning. A 40 percent jump in token consumption is rarely a billing problem. It is almost always a product problem wearing a billing costume: a prompt that grew, a context window that quietly tripled, a router that started sending easy questions to expensive models.

In my own stack, the first time I opened the Command Center and saw a real feed of token usage across active sessions, the number that caught me was not the spend. It was the variance. Two ostensibly identical tasks, run ten minutes apart, were burning wildly different amounts. One took a 2,000-token detour through a tool registry to answer something the base model already knew. The other did the same job in 400 tokens. The model had not changed. The prompt had not changed. The routing had.

This is the moment the frontier becomes visible. Tokens are not just consumed, they are spent on choices, and the choices compound.

What a token-efficiency frontier actually is

Borrowed from production economics, a frontier is the set of configurations where you cannot improve one outcome (quality, latency, capability) without sacrificing another (cost, speed, determinism). For LLMs, the token-efficiency frontier is the curve of best-possible quality-per-token at each capability tier. Every point on the curve is a configuration you have already considered: model, prompt template, retrieval depth, tool list, context window, caching strategy, post-processing.

A point below the curve is waste. A point above the curve does not exist in your current system. To move the frontier itself, you have to change something structural: a fine-tune, a new model, a smarter router, a different data shape. Most PMs spend their time arguing about points on the curve, when the leverage is in moving the curve.

The framework has three moves: (1) find where you are, (2) climb to the frontier, (3) push the frontier out.

Three variables in tension

Every configuration is a bet across three variables, and the bet is the entire game.

Capability required. What does the task actually need? Classifying a support ticket into one of eight categories is a different problem from drafting a nuanced escalation email. A PM who treats these as the same problem will overspend on the first and underspend on the second.

Context size. More context is not always better. Past a certain point, models get distracted, hallucinate edges, and burn tokens reading material they will not use. The instinct to "just dump the whole doc" is the most common frontier-violation I see.

Model tier. Cheaper models are not just cheaper. They are differently capable. They fail in different places. The right question is not "which model is cheapest" but "which model clears the capability bar for this specific task with the smallest context."

The frontier is where these three are jointly optimal. Move any one without checking the others, and you fall off.

A worked example from my own stack

I run a multi-service local stack: a chat gateway on port 8642 that streams completions and exposes models, a dashboard API on port 9119 that handles sessions, skills, memory, and orchestration, and a self-hosted Postiz instance on port 4007 for content scheduling. On top of that sits a Google Workspace MCP that connects three Gmail accounts (saghir.sahil as the primary, plus sahilsaghir.ss9 and fusionfirststudios) and a Command Center that surfaces token usage across all of it.

Last month I shipped a feature: a "daily digest" agent that summarises unread mail across all three accounts and drafts replies for the ones that look routine. The first version routed every message through the largest model with the full thread history attached. Quality was fine. Token spend was not. I opened Command Center, looked at the activity feed, and saw roughly 70 percent of the tokens going to messages that were either automated notifications or one-line acknowledgements that needed no draft at all.

I climbed to the frontier in three steps. First, I added a cheap classifier in front of the agent: short, low-context, fast. If the message was notification-shaped, it got a one-line summary and exited the pipeline. Second, I tightened the context window for the drafter: not the full thread, only the last two messages plus the thread subject. Third, I moved the routine acknowledgement drafts to a smaller model, and reserved the large model for the 20 percent of messages that actually needed nuance. Quality on those held steady. Quality on the boring 80 percent was never the bottleneck, so nothing visible got worse.

The frontier moved because the router got smarter, not because any single model got cheaper.

The trade-offs nobody warns you about

There are three honest costs to this framework that I do not see acknowledged often enough.

First, observability is not free. To know where you are on the frontier, you have to log per-task token usage, model choice, prompt version, and outcome quality. That is a real engineering investment. Without it, the frontier is a story you tell yourself.

Second, the frontier is not stable. New models drop. Pricing changes. A prompt template that was optimal in March is suboptimal in May. Treating the frontier as a fixed target is how teams end up with a "tuning" meeting every quarter and no actual movement.

Third, the framework is unkind to simple workflows. If your product is a single prompt with a single model, the frontier collapses to a point and the framework is overhead. The framework earns its keep when there is a router, multiple models, multiple task types, or any meaningful context engineering. Below that threshold, just pick a reasonable model and move on.

How to apply this

A practical rollout, in order, with no shortcuts.

Step 1: Instrument per-task token usage. Not total spend. Per-task, per-model, per-prompt-version. The Command Center pattern, where a single activity feed shows every call with its cost, is the right shape. If you cannot see it, you cannot optimise it.

Step 2: Define capability bars for each task type. Not "good enough." A specific bar: "must not hallucinate account numbers", "must draft in under 200 words", "must not suggest actions outside the approved tool list." Bars are what let you swap models confidently.

Step 3: Identify the worst off-frontier offender. Look for the task consuming the most tokens for the least quality lift. In my stack it was the unconditional full-thread context. In most stacks it is a retrieval pipeline that returns too much, or a tool list that has grown without pruning.

Step 4: Move one knob at a time, but check all three. When you change the prompt, watch the model tier implication. When you change the model, watch the context implication. When you change the context, watch the capability implication. A change in one variable is rarely a change in one variable.

Step 5: Re-measure on a fixed cadence. Weekly, at minimum. The frontier drifts.

What I'd try next

The piece I have not yet built, and which I now think is the next leverage point, is a small "frontier dashboard" sitting alongside Command Center. It would plot, for each task type, the actual quality score against the actual token cost, for the last 30 days. Points below the curve become a backlog. Points on the curve become a baseline. The work shifts from arguing about which model to use, to arguing about which curve to push out next, which is a better argument to have.

The second thing I would try is a deliberate "context diet" week, where every prompt is reviewed and trimmed without changing capability bars, and the savings are banked. Most stacks have 20 to 30 percent of context that is doing no measurable work. Finding it is mostly reading and resisting the urge to add more.

Reflection

I have come around to the view that the biggest mistake PMs make with LLMs is treating tokens as a cost line and quality as a product line, as if they lived in different rooms. They do not. They share a curve, and the curve is the product, in a way that is not true of most infrastructure. A team that cannot talk fluently about where they are on that curve, and why, will ship features that look smart and feel expensive in equal measure. The framework is not complicated. The discipline of using it is. The teams that win the next few years will be the ones that treat token efficiency as a product surface, with its own backlog, its own review meetings, and its own owners. The ones that do not will keep paying for capability they are not using, and calling it innovation.
